Introducing
Owl 3

RD Framework JS - Géry Debongnie

Why Owl 3?

Scaling Odoo JS: challenges in taming complexity

The frontier

Rendering is a solved problem.

React, Vue, Solid, Owl — every one of them will put your state on screen efficiently. Nobody switches framework for rendering any more.

The diagnosis

Fighting Complexity

The places where a codebase this size started to press against the framework.

  • 1

    Reactivity that is subtle to get right

    Simple on the surface; hard-to-diagnose bugs underneath, as workflows got more complex.

  • 2

    Hard to write fast derived state

    Caches, getters, onWillRender precomputes — "sadly, they usually do not compose well".

  • 3

    No typing or autocompletion

    For props and for env. Hence years of hand-written and generated .d.ts files.

  • 4

    No guidance on how to build an app

    "It is nice not to be constrained, but it makes it more difficult to understand other parts of the codebase."

The frontier

Next challenge:
State management

  • Describing state
  • Deriving one value from another
  • Recomputing efficiently
  • Reacting to change
  • Sharing it, without one part owning another
  • All of that, but asynchronously
  • …

The shift

A change of paradigm

The centre of the framework moves. Rendering stops being the thing everything is arranged around, and state takes its place.

The component tree has not gone anywhere. But the important part is the state relationships

Getting the balance right

  • Not enough power → every team invents its own solution, and none of them compose.
  • Too much power → code spends its life working around the framework.

Signals

State management inside the computation graph.

Example

Computing a derived value

  • An expensive value, precomputed once per render, cached by hand.
  • It works. It is also four moving parts held together by convention.

Owl 2

class Dashboard extends Component {
    setup() {
        this.state = useState({ total: 0 });

        onWillRender(() => {
            const key = this.props.orders.length;
            if (key !== this._key) {
                this._key = key;
                this._total = expensive(this.props.orders);
            }
            this.state.total = this._total;
        });
    }
}
  • Four partsA hook, a hand-rolled cache key, a private field, and a piece of state to write into.
  • The ruleNothing in the code says total depends on orders. That fact lives in your head.
  • And thenAnother addon patches expensive, or adds a second input. The cache key is now wrong, silently.

The dependency was never written down.

It lived implicitly, in a set of closures and some unconnected pieces of state. The framework could not see it — so the framework could not help.

Spoiler:Owl 3 lets us make the state explicit, computed values included.

Reactivity: signal

  • A value of its own: call it to read, set it to write.
  • No proxy, no wrapper object, nothing to unwrap.

counter.js

import { Component, signal } from "@odoo/owl";

class Counter extends Component {
    static template = "my_module.Counter";

    counter = signal(0);

    increment() {
        this.counter.set(this.counter() + 1);
    }
}

counter.xml

<t t-name="my_module.Counter">
    <p>
      Counter: <t t-out="this.counter()"/>
    </p>
    <button t-on-click="this.increment">
      Increment
    </button>
</t>

Reactivity

Computations

Can manage dependencies. Three kinds, and one mechanism under all of them: each reads signals, and re-runs when what it read changes.

  • 1

    Rendering a component

    Reads signals, writes DOM. This is the one you already have.

  • 2

    A computed value

    Reads signals, returns a value, and holds on to it until one of them changes.

  • 3

    An effect

    Reads signals, and changes something outside the graph: the document, storage, a library that knows nothing about this one.

A render is not a special case. It is a computation that happens to paint.

Derived values

computed

  • The same expensive value, with the same caching, in one declaration.

Owl 2 — four moving parts

setup() {
    this.state = useState({ total: 0 });

    onWillRender(() => {
        const key = this.props.orders.length;
        if (key !== this._key) {
            this._key = key;
            this._total = expensive(this.props.orders);
        }
        this.state.total = this._total;
    });
}

Owl 3 — one

total = computed(() =>
    expensive(this.props.orders)
);
  • CachedIt does not recompute unless something it read changed.
  • DeclaredThe dependency is now written down. The runtime can see it.

The trigger moved: Owl 2 recomputed because a component was about to render, Owl 3 because the state it read changed.

Derived values

computed is fast by construction

You get the caching you used to hand-roll, and this time it composes.

  • FreeMemoisation comes with the primitive. Nobody writes a cache key, so nobody gets the cache key wrong.
  • LazyA computed that nothing reads never runs at all.
  • GatedThe propagation stops when the value does not change — not merely when the input does.
  • ComposableA computed reading another computed just works, and keeps working when another addon patches either one.

This is soft limit 2, answered. How the graph actually pulls it off is my other talk.

Effects

useEffect

  • The same tracking, pointed outwards: at the document, at storage, at a library that knows nothing about signals.

counter.js

setup() {
    useEffect(() => {
        document.title = `Counter: ${this.counter()}`;
    });
}
  • Nothing to declareIt read counter, so it re-runs when counter changes.
  • Runs firstThe first run is how it finds out what it reads.
  • Then batchedA burst of writes costs one run, after the microtask.
  • DisposedIt goes when the component goes.

A computed gives you a value. An effect changes something outside the graph.

Effects

A value, or a change to the world

  • Both track what they read, and both re-run when it changes.
  • What differs is what you want out of them.

computed — you want a value

remaining = computed(() =>
    this.todos().filter(
        (t) => !t.completed()
    ).length
);

Read it like a signal. Never set it. No side effect, ever.

useEffect — you want a side effect

useEffect(() => {
    localStorage.setItem(
        "todos", serialize(this.todos()),
    );
});

Saving, logging, a third-party library. Returns nothing useful.

When in doubt, start with computed. Reach for an effect when something outside Owl has to change.

Signals

Four kinds of signal, one tracker

Pick by the shape of your data, not by taste.

  • signal(0)

    A single value

    Tracks the value.

  • signal.Array([])

    A list you add to

    Tracks its own items, shallow.

  • signal.Object({})

    A flat bag of keys

    Tracks its own keys, shallow.

  • proxy({ ... })

    A nested tree of settings

    Tracks every level, recursively.

The collection signals are shallow: what is inside stays plain, and stays untracked. That is the one gotcha.

Plugins

State management across the component tree.

The problem

What was wrong with env

The same diagnosis, one level up. env was under-powered, so every team invented a convention on top of it — and none of them composed.

Owl 2

// one bag, for everything
this.env.services.action
this.env.bus
this.env.debug

// a service, reached by string
this.orm = useService("orm");

// and state handed down invisibly
useSubEnv({ myCounter: this.counter });
  • UntypedA string key into a bag. No autocompletion, no rename, no way to find the callers.
  • InvisibleuseSubEnv changed what a subtree saw, from a distance, with nothing at the other end to say so.
  • UnboundedAnything could reach anything. Which meant everything eventually did.

This is soft limit 3 and soft limit 4, in one object.

Plugins

A plugin is a class

  • Reactive state, methods, and a lifecycle of its own: setup, then destroy.
  • One instance, shared by everyone who asks for it.

clock_plugin.js

import { Plugin, signal, onWillDestroy } from "@odoo/owl";

export class Clock extends Plugin {
    now = signal(new Date());

    setup() {
        const id = setInterval(
            () => this.now.set(new Date()), 1000,
        );
        onWillDestroy(() => clearInterval(id));
    }
}

two components, one interval

class DigitalClock extends Component {
    clock = usePlugin(Clock);
}

class UtcClock extends Component {
    clock = usePlugin(Clock);
}

digital_clock.xml

<t t-name="my_module.DigitalClock">
    <span t-out="this.clock.now().toLocaleTimeString()"/>
</t>

In sync, and one interval however many clocks mount.

Hooks work inside a plugin too: useEffect, useListener, onWillStart.

Plugins

Asked for by class, not by name

This is the whole typing story, and it is why plugins replace env rather than sitting beside it.

Owl 2

// a string. hope you spelled it right
this.orm = useService("orm");

// what does it return? see the .d.ts
this.orm.searchRead(/* ... */);

Owl 3

import { ORM } from "@web/core/orm_plugin";

// a class. the editor knows the type
orm = usePlugin(ORM);

orm.searchRead(/* autocompleted */);

Rename the file, move the class, find every caller — all the things an import gives you and a string never did.

Soft limit 3, answered: no generated .d.ts, because the class is the type.

Plugins

Where a plugin lives

The class is the same. The line that installs it decides who can reach it, and for how long.

State that must outlive a screen goes global. Everything else stays on the screen that owns it.

Plugins

Dependencies

  • A plugin reaches another by calling usePlugin — in a class field, or in setup.

statistics_plugin.js

export class StatisticsPlugin extends Plugin {
    orm = usePlugin(ORM);

    stats = signal.Object({});

    setup() {
        onWillStart(async () => {
            this.stats.set(await this.orm.call(
                "res.partner", "get_statistics"));
        });
    }
}
  • By classNot a name in a dependencies array. Rename the file and nothing breaks.
  • AsynconWillStart in a plugin holds back the first render, so a component can read stats straight away.
  • Sequencestatic sequence = 10 for the few that everything else reads. Default 50, lower first.

Plugins

Services become plugins

  • A global plugin is exactly a service, with a class instead of a string.

@web/core/services.js — the whole file

import { Plugin, Resource, types as t } from "@odoo/owl";

export const services = new Resource({
    name: "services",
    validation: t.constructor(Plugin),
});

The service registry is itself a Resource. Every global plugin lands in it.

and to register one

import { services } from "@web/core/services";

export class TitlePlugin extends Plugin { /* ... */ }

services.add(TitlePlugin);
  • TodaySome twenty plugins in addons/web, against some thirty-five services still in the old shape.

Write plugins. Read both — useService is still all over the codebase, and will be for a while.

Other changes

The smaller things, and what they each take off your hands.

Other changes

Rendering context

  • A template used to resolve a bare name against the component, its props and its own t-set variables, in that order. Now this. says which one you meant.

Owl 2

<t t-name="my_module.Counter">
    <t t-set="double" t-value="counter * 2"/>
    <p>
        Counter: <t t-out="counter"/>,
        double: <t t-out="double"/>
    </p>
    <button t-on-click="increment">+1</button>
</t>

Owl 3

<t t-name="my_module.Counter">
    <t t-set="double" t-value="this.counter() * 2"/>
    <p>
        Counter: <t t-out="this.counter()"/>,
        double: <t t-out="double"/>
    </p>
    <button t-on-click="this.increment">+1</button>
</t>

A name your editor can follow back to a class field is a name it can check.

Other changes

useProps

  • useProps is a view over the props: the same values the parent passed, read through signals, with the shape you expect written next to them.

Owl 2

static props = {
    count: Number,
    items: { type: Array, element: Object },
    onSelect: { type: Function, optional: true },
};

// this.props.count
// a schema your editor cannot read

Owl 3

props = useProps({
    count: t.number(),
    items: t.array(t.object({ id: t.number() })),
    onSelect: t.function().optional(),
    size: t.selection(["small", "large"]),
});
  • Per keySignal-backed. Reading this.props.count subscribes you to that prop alone.
  • CheckedOn create and on update, in dev mode. useProps() bare takes anything; useProps(["count"]) just names the keys.

Other changes

A ref is now a signal too

  • No separate useRef concept: signal.ref() is a signal that starts at null.
  • t-model takes one as well, and binds it both ways.

todo_list.js

import { signal, computed, useEffect } from "@odoo/owl";

export class TodoList extends Component {
    input = signal.ref();
    name = signal("");

    greeting = computed(() => `Hello ${this.name()}`);

    setup() {
        useEffect(() => this.input()?.focus());
    }
}

todo_list.xml

<input t-ref="this.input"
       placeholder="What needs doing?"/>

<input t-model="this.name"/>
<p t-out="this.greeting()"/>

One concept fewer to hold: refs, model bindings and state are all the same thing - so a computed reads what t-model writes, with nothing in between.

Read it like any other signal — this.input() — and it is null until the component is mounted.

The change surface

Gone, new, and changed

The same change, as the words you actually type.

gone

  • useState
  • reactive
  • toRaw
  • useComponent
  • useRef
  • onWillRender
  • onRendered
  • onWillUpdateProps
  • this.render
  • env
  • useSubEnv
  • services
  • t-esc

new

  • signal
  • signal.Array
  • signal.Object
  • signal.ref
  • proxy
  • computed
  • asyncComputed
  • useOnChange
  • untrack
  • Plugin
  • usePlugin
  • providePlugins
  • useScope
  • useProps
  • assertType
  • validateType

changed

  • t-slot → t-call-slot
  • useExternalListener → useListener
  • useEffect reads, not a deps array
  • t-ref a signal, not a name
  • t-model binds a signal

This list may or may not be exhaustive.

The change surface

The same component, twice

Owl 2

class OrderSummary extends Component {
    static props = {
        orders: Array,
        currency: { type: String, optional: true },
    };
    static defaultProps = { currency: "USD" };

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.state = useState({ total: 0 });
        onWillRender(() => {
            this.state.total = sumAmounts(this.props.orders);
        });
    }

    validate() {
        return this.orm.call("sale.order", "confirm",
            [this.props.orders.map((o) => o.id)]);
    }
}
<t t-name="sale.OrderSummary">
    <p t-esc="state.total"/>
    <button t-on-click="validate">Validate</button>
</t>

Owl 3

class OrderSummary extends Component {
    props = useProps({
        orders: t.array(t.object()),
        currency: t.string().optional(() => "USD"),
    });

    orm = usePlugin(ORM);

    total = computed(() => sumAmounts(this.props.orders));

    validate() {
        return this.orm.call("sale.order", "confirm",
            [this.props.orders.map((o) => o.id)]);
    }
}
<t t-name="sale.OrderSummary">
    <p t-out="this.total()"/>
    <button t-on-click="this.validate">Validate</button>
</t>

Migration

Everyone loves migrating code.

Migration

No big deal.
We have AIs now.

The transition

Migration

You are not doing this by reading diffs.

  • Release notes

    Every breaking change written down, version by version, with what to write instead of it.

  • Migration scripts

    The mechanical half, run over your addon: the renames, the imports, the template syntax.

Which is how the syntax migration got finished. The architecture is the half that is still yours.

The transition

The syntax migration is finished.
The architecture migration is a third done.

Nobody is writing useState any more. Plenty of code still reaches for this.env, and that is the work that remains.

  • The layer@web/owl2/* puts this.env, useSubEnv, onWillRender and friends back. 194 files import it today.
  • TemporaryIt goes as soon as it can. Code that leans on it goes with it, so do not write new code against it.
  • Owl itself3.0.0-alpha.48, in a correctness and hardening phase rather than a feature phase.
  • HonestlyOdoo runs on it. That is the strongest statement available, and it is a real one.

An alpha that the whole product already runs on is a different animal from an alpha nobody uses.

The transition

Which version runs what

  • Not compatibleOwl 3 does not run Owl 2 code. They are separate libraries.
  • PerformanceNot slower. Somewhat faster, and faster still once code is actually written with signals. That is not why we did it.

Odoo 19.0 stays on Owl 2 for its whole life. Nothing you have shipped is going to move under you.

Where this goes

And where to find all of it.

Closing the loop

What Owl 3 gives you

Three sets of tools against complexity — between them, the four soft limits from the start of the talk.

  • signal · computed · useEffect

    Reactivity belongs to the value, not to the container it arrived in, so it survives every boundary. Derived state declares itself: lazy, cached, composing across addons. An effect is a thing you write, not a lifecycle hook you hang code on.

    Still coming: asyncComputed, Suspense, cancellation that follows the component that asked for it.

  • Plugin · usePlugin

    Shared logic asked for by class, not by a string nobody can follow back to its source. Global, or owned by the screen that opened it — the framework finally has an opinion about where logic lives.

    Still coming: Owl stops being one library and becomes a small family — a router, an ORM.

  • useProps · types

    Props say their own shape, and a plugin's class is its own type. That is years of hand-written and generated .d.ts files no longer worth writing.

Go and read it

odoo.github.io/owl

Documentation, versioned. A playground that needs nothing installed. Three tutorials.

Appendix

Held in reserve, for the questions that come.

If it comes up

Performance

It is not in the talk on purpose. Rendering is a solved problem, and arguing render timings would undercut the slide that says so.

  • Equivalent codeBenchmarks put Owl 3 about level with Owl 2, or a little ahead.
  • Code that uses computedFaster, and the gap widens with how much of the work is derived rather than recomputed.
  • SoSpeed is a consequence of the design, not the reason for it.

If it comes up

Why not just move to React?

Because the balance point is not universal. It is Odoo's own.

  • Addons patch what we ship

    Templates inherited by xpath, components patched at runtime, by modules Odoo does not write. React has no equivalent, and no reason to want one.

  • 4,000 JS files

    Many teams, plus every custom module in the wild. A rewrite breaks code that is not ours to fix.

  • Owl solves Odoo problems

    Writing extensible code. Runtime compiling. Dynamic bundles …

Extensibility

Replacing a plugin

A child providePlugins carrying the same static id shadows the parent's — for that subtree, and only there.

theme_plugin.js

export class ThemePlugin extends Plugin {
    static id = "theme";  // defaults to the class name
    color = "light";
}

// in another addon
export class DarkTheme extends Plugin {
    static id = "theme";  // the same id: it shadows
    color = "dark";
}

class DarkSection extends Component {
    setup() {
        providePlugins([DarkTheme]);
    }
}
  • ScopedBelow DarkSection, usePlugin(ThemePlugin) hands back the dark one. Elsewhere nothing changes.
  • CompareThe registry answer to the same problem is { force: true } — global, and permanent.

An override that cannot leak out of the subtree that asked for it.
